content_voiceover: This is the manual polybrene method, commonly used in Taiwan for antibody screening. Polybrene is a cationic, positively charged polymer that neutralizes the red cell's normal negative surface charge, the zeta potential, which normally keeps red cells apart and prevents IgG antibodies from bridging them directly. Step one, add low ionic medium, or LIM, to enhance antibody-antigen binding. Step two, add polybrene and centrifuge; this creates nonspecific aggregation regardless of whether antibody is present, because the neutralized charge lets any red cells clump together. Step three, add citrate to neutralize the polybrene's charge. If the only cause was nonspecific charge neutralization, the aggregates disperse; but if a true antigen-antibody reaction occurred, the agglutination persists because antibody is physically bridging the cells. By protocol, nonspecific aggregation should disperse within ten seconds; true agglutination will not fully disperse. If the reaction looks weak or borderline, you can confirm under a microscope.
keypoints: Polybrene, a cationic polymer, neutralizes RBC negative surface charge, causing nonspecific aggregation.
Step 1: LIM enhances antibody binding. Step 2: polybrene plus spin causes clumping. Step 3: citrate reverses nonspecific aggregation.
True antibody-antigen agglutination persists after citrate; nonspecific clumping disperses within 10 seconds.
Microscope can confirm weak or equivocal reactions.
